title: Lost the Original Sale Deed? How to Get a Certified Copy and Protect Your Title
meta_description: What to do if you lose the original sale deed: police report, public notice, indemnity bond, and getting a certified copy from the registration office.
intro: Losing the original sale deed is alarming but it is not, on its own, a loss of title. Ownership rests on the registered instrument recorded in the sub-registrar's books, not on the physical sheet of paper you happen to hold. As on today's date, every owner who loses an original deed can apply to the sub-registrar's office where it was registered and obtain a certified copy under Section 57 of the Registration Act, 1908, which the registering officer is required to furnish on payment of the prescribed fee.

That said, a certified copy is not a perfect substitute for the original, and buyers, banks and courts treat it with more caution. This guide sets out the practical sequence lawyers advise in this situation: a report to the police, a public notice, a notarised affidavit and indemnity bond, and then the application to the registration office, along with what the certified copy can and cannot do for you afterward. For the separate question of how to check a property's title before buying it, see our title due diligence guide.

sections.heading: First, report the loss
paragraphs: The usual first step is a written complaint to the local police station recording that the original sale deed has been lost or misplaced. Practice on whether this must be a formal FIR or can be a non-cognizable (NC) entry varies by state and by police station, since loss of a private document is not itself a cognizable offence in most circumstances; some stations will register an NC entry and hand over an acknowledged copy, which is usually enough for the steps that follow. Keep the original complaint receipt or the NC report copy, since it will be annexed to the application you eventually make to the sub-registrar and is often asked for by banks and buyers later.

If the deed was lost along with other identity or property documents, for instance in theft, fire or flood, mention this plainly in the complaint, since insurers and the registration office may ask for the same report for other claims as well.

sections.heading: Public notice and the indemnity bond
paragraphs: A public notice is then published, ordinarily in one local and one widely circulated newspaper, stating that the original sale deed for the specific property has been lost and inviting anyone with the document, or with a claim or objection, to come forward within a stated period. This step exists to protect a future buyer or lender against the risk that the lost original surfaces in someone else's hands, or that the loss itself is a cover for some other dispute over the property.

Alongside the notice, the owner typically executes a notarised affidavit describing the circumstances of the loss, and an indemnity bond on stamp paper undertaking to indemnify a future buyer, bank or other person who deals with the property against any loss arising from the missing original. Stamp duty on the indemnity bond is modest and varies by state, so check the current rate with a local stamp vendor or the sub-registrar's office rather than assuming a fixed figure. Banks financing a purchase or accepting the property as security will usually insist on seeing the police report, the newspaper cutting and the indemnity bond together, not the certified copy alone.

sections.heading: Applying for a certified copy under the Registration Act
paragraphs: Section 57 of the Registration Act, 1908 obliges the registering officer to allow inspection of the registration books and to give certified copies of any entry to the person who executed or claims under the document, on payment of the prescribed fees. The application is made at the sub-registrar's office where the deed was originally registered, since every registered document is permanently preserved in that office's books. You will usually need the registration number, book and volume details, or the year of registration and the parties' names if you cannot recall the exact numbers, since the office will have to locate the entry before it can certify a copy.

The certified copy carries the registering officer's signature and seal and reproduces the contents of the deed as recorded in the books. It is not a replacement original, and the Registration Act does not provide a mechanism for re-registering a lost private document in the way it allows for certified copies of court decrees; what you get is proof of what the original said, not a new original.

sections.heading: What the certified copy proves, and what it does not
paragraphs: In a dispute, a certified copy of a registered sale deed is ordinarily admissible as secondary evidence of the document's contents once the loss of the original is established, a principle carried forward under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, which replaced the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, from 1 July 2024. Secondary evidence provisions let a court accept the certified copy once the party explains why the original cannot be produced, but the explanation itself, including the police report and the public notice, matters to how readily a court accepts it.

What the certified copy does not do is create a fresh chain of title or cure any underlying defect in the deed itself. If the sale deed being copied was itself defective, under-stamped, or part of a disputed chain, the certified copy inherits exactly the same weaknesses. Possession of the paper, original or certified copy, has never been what makes someone the owner; the underlying transfer and the record of it do that. Someone who happens to be holding your original deed, for whatever reason, does not become the owner merely by having the paper.

sections.heading: Practical effect on a pending sale or mortgage
paragraphs: If you are mid-transaction when you discover the deed is missing, tell the buyer or the bank immediately rather than trying to complete the deal quietly. A buyer's lawyer doing reasonable diligence will usually ask for the original at some stage, and discovering the loss later, after money has changed hands, invites exactly the kind of dispute the public notice and indemnity bond are meant to head off before it happens. Most buyers and banks will proceed on the strength of the certified copy, the police report, the notice and the indemnity bond together, provided the rest of the title chain is otherwise clean.

Where a bank itself is the one that has lost your title documents, for instance after loan closure, the position is different and generally more favourable to the owner: the bank is expected to bear the cost and process of obtaining the certified copy and any compensation for demonstrable loss, rather than the owner being left to run the entire process at their own expense.

faqs.q: Is a police FIR compulsory before I can get a certified copy of a lost sale deed?
faqs.a: Practice differs by state and police station. Many stations record a non-cognizable report rather than a full FIR for the loss of a private document, and that report copy is usually enough for the sub-registrar's office and for buyers or banks later. Check with your local station what it will issue.

faqs.q: Does a certified copy of my sale deed give me the same rights as the original?
faqs.a: It proves the contents of the original and can be used as secondary evidence once the loss is properly explained, but it is not a fresh original and does not cure any defect that existed in the underlying deed. Your ownership rests on the registered transfer itself, not on possession of the paper.

faqs.q: Can someone else claim my property just because they have found my lost sale deed?
faqs.a: No. Ownership of registered immovable property does not pass merely by possession of the paper document. The registered transfer and the record in the sub-registrar's books are what establish title, which is also why the public notice step exists, to flush out any genuine competing claim rather than leave it hidden.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a certified copy from the sub-registrar's office?
faqs.a: Timelines vary by state and by how quickly the office can locate the entry in its books, which is faster if you can supply the registration number, book and volume, or at least the approximate year and the parties' names. Treat any timeline a private guide quotes as indicative only and confirm the current practice with your local office.

references: Registration Act, 1908, Section 57, on inspection of registration books and certified copies

General registration-office practice on certified copies of lost sale deeds as secondary evidence of their contents
verification_notes: Section 57 of the Registration Act requiring the registering officer to furnish certified copies on payment of fees: confirmed from the India Code text of the Act and from secondary commentary (sansalegal, jurigram) describing the same right and procedure in near-identical terms.

The sequence of police report, public notice, notarised affidavit and indemnity bond before approaching the sub-registrar: confirmed across three independent practitioner guides (sansalegal, righttoinformation.wiki, jurigram) describing the same four-step sequence, though these are secondary blog sources rather than official procedure, and this is flagged in the body text.

That Section 67 of the Registration Act was omitted by the 2001 amendment, and that the Act has no express mechanism to re-register a lost private document the way it does for court decree copies: confirmed from lawgist.in's section-wise text and a 2015-dated case commentary (lawweb.in) making the same point about decrees versus private documents.

Certified copies as secondary evidence under the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, replacing the Indian Evidence Act from 1 July 2024: the specific BSA section number corresponding to the old Evidence Act secondary-evidence provisions was not independently confirmed in the search results, so this guide states the principle in general terms and names the governing statute and its commencement date without citing an unverified section number.

Stamp duty on the indemnity bond being a modest, state-variable figure: one source suggested a specific rupee range for one state; since this was not confirmed from a second source and rates differ by state, this guide states only that the amount is modest and state-specific rather than naming a figure.

Bank practice on bearing costs where the bank itself lost the owner's documents: this reflects general consumer-protection practice reported in secondary sources (outlookbusiness, community.verified.realestate) rather than a specific statute, and is stated as general practice rather than a guaranteed entitlement.
